title: Interest Is Owed on a Security Deposit
bodyText:
The city requires interest on a residential security deposit (B.R.C. 1981 sections 12-2-5 to 12-2-7). A security deposit is any advance or deposit of money, whatever it's called, whose main purpose is to secure performance of the rental agreement (section 12-2-2), so a pet deposit can count. The interest is simple interest on the full deposit. The city manager sets the rate each December from one-year certificates of deposit and publishes it, and it applies to deposits provided in the next calendar year. For a tenancy of more than one year, figure the interest separately for each year, using the city's list of prior rates and its formula. Under a lease entered into before March 19, 2004, the rate is 5.5 percent a year.

For residential property regulated by state law, the deposit stays the tenant's property. After the tenancy you may keep it or its interest only for actual cause under state law. The city's rule creates a duty to account for the interest, not a fiduciary relationship.

Before the tenant moves in, the written lease, rental agreement, site rules or other document you sign and give must say that interest must be paid on the deposit (section 12-2-4(a)(1)(F)). The penalty for violating section 12-2-4 is at most $500 for all violations charged in a single court proceeding.

Return the accrued interest within one month after the lease ends or the home is surrendered and accepted, whichever is later, following state law on returning the deposit and on notice and legality of deductions. Any interest that builds up after that is due when you return the deposit. State law lets a lease allow up to 60 days for the deposit, but the city section doesn't say that extends the month, so pay interest within the month.

If you keep any interest without giving the notice state law requires for keeping a deposit, you lose the right to keep any of the interest. Willfully and wrongfully keeping interest makes whoever holds the deposit (you, or a manager holding it) liable to the tenant for $100 or three times the amount kept, whichever is more, plus reasonable attorney's fees and court costs, if the tenant gave at least seven days' notice before filing. In a tenant's suit under the city's rules the holder must prove that keeping the interest wasn't a violation, and the tenant can bring state and city claims in the same lawsuit. Wrongfully keeping the deposit itself has its own state penalties. A written or oral term waiving these rules is void (section 12-2-8).

Exception: sections 12-2-5 and 12-2-6 (ownership, return, penalties and burden of proof) don't apply to a deposit paid to a mobile home park for the lease of a mobile home space. State law has the park hold it in a separate trust account and lets the park keep the interest (C.R.S. 38-12-207).
notes: B.R.C. 12-2-2, -4(a)(1)(F), -5 to -8 read; C.R.S. 38-12-103(1)(a). Not decided: whether the general penalty 5-2-4 also applies to 12-2-6(a). City page's 2026 rate and its lease-signing-date reading not adopted: the code ties the rate to the year the deposit is provided. title: A Written Lease and Copies to Each Tenant
bodyText:
If you rent residential property for 30 days or more, enter into a written lease within 30 days after the rental begins (B.R.C. 1981 section 12-2-3). Don't rely on the 30 days: before anyone occupies the rental, you must also have signed and given the tenant a written lease, rental agreement, site rules or other document with the city's required disclosures, and must keep an accurate list of the people authorized to live there (section 12-2-4).

Give each tenant a copy of the lease within seven working days after it is fully signed, or within fifteen working days after any tenant signs, whichever comes first. State law separately requires a copy signed by both of you by the seventh day after the tenant signs (C.R.S. 38-12-801), so meet whichever deadline comes first.

Before a summons and complaint under section 12-2-3, the complaining witness or a city peace officer must first request a copy of the lease, and you have five working days from the mailing or delivery of that request to provide it. A written or oral term waiving these rules is void (section 12-2-8). Violating section 12-2-4 carries at most $500 for all violations charged in a single court proceeding. Section 12-2-3 sets no penalty of its own, so the city's general penalty (section 5-2-4) appears to apply: a fine, and jail only if the violation was intentional, knowing or reckless.

title: No Renting a Building Heated Only by a Solid Fuel Stove
bodyText:
You may not rent out a building if a solid fuel burning device is its sole source of heat (B.R.C. 1981 section 6-9-6). The code's definition of sole source of heat speaks of woodstoves that are the only heating, so treat fireplaces, pellet stoves and other solid fuel devices the same way. A building doesn't count if it has a permanently installed furnace or heating system that uses oil, natural gas, electricity or propane, even one disconnected from its energy source (section 6-9-2). That exception answers only this city rule: state law still requires working heat (C.R.S. 38-12-505).

Any penalty falls on the owner, not the tenant. The fine is up to $100 for a first conviction, $200 for a second and $300 for a third, looking back two years (section 6-9-7).

title: A Working Toilet and Sewage System Is the Owner's Duty
bodyText:
The county's septic system regulations, which cover the whole county including its cities, make the owner of any structure where people live responsible for an adequate, convenient, sanitary toilet and sewage system in good working order (Weld County Code sections 30-1-20 and 30-4-10). Whether that also reaches a home on public sewer isn't clear, because the regulations say they apply to on-site systems (section 30-2-10), so treat it as applying. The regulations cover systems designed for up to 2,000 gallons a day; larger ones need state site approval, design review and a discharge permit.

Sewage or effluent may not be discharged onto the ground or into state waters unless it meets the regulations' minimum requirements or state water quality standards, whichever apply (section 30-4-10). No one may build or maintain a dwelling without adequate sewage disposal; a failed septic system, or a condition the local health agency determines is a public health or safety concern, doesn't count as adequate. Cesspools, pit privies, slit trenches and seepage pits are prohibited. Don't connect more than one dwelling or other unit to the same septic system unless the application and permit specified it (section 30-4-140).

The owner or occupant must let the county in at reasonable times, on reasonable notice, to inspect, test, sample and monitor a septic system; if refused, the county may ask the District Court for an order (section 30-4-60). The county addresses written violation notices to the owner, with a reasonable time to correct. Separately, the owner or occupant must apply for a repair permit within two business days after getting notice that the system isn't working in compliance or is a nuisance or public health hazard, and a permit is needed before any repair; the county may allow emergency use meanwhile (section 30-4-30; C.R.S. 25-10-106(1)(j)). If the health officer finds a system out of compliance, a public health hazard or not repaired in time, then after a hearing on at least 48 hours' written notice the officer may order the owner or occupant to fix it within at most 30 days or stop using it; a petition to the district court must be filed within ten days after the order. On finding a violation, the board of health may assess up to $50 for each day; you may ask the board for a hearing within 30 days after the penalty is assessed (sections 30-4-160 and 30-4-170; C.R.S. 25-10-113). Letting a septic system be used without the required permit, violating a final order, or breaking the state on-site wastewater law, which bars maintaining a dwelling without adequate sewage disposal, is a civil infraction with a fine of up to $100 (C.R.S. 25-10-113 and 18-1.3-503).

title: Septic Maintenance Is the Owner's Unless a Contract Assigns It
bodyText:
The county makes the owner responsible for maintaining a septic system unless a contract assigns that to a tenant, another party or a public body (Weld County Code section 30-13-10). This applies in the cities too (section 30-1-20). Section 30-4-10 separately requires the owner to ensure a working system and has no exception for a contract.

State law is stricter. Where the work is needed to keep a home habitable, you can move only specific tasks to the tenant, and only for a single-family residence for which you get no government subsidy, in good faith, in a signed writing separate from the lease, with adequate consideration, if the tenant has the skills to do it, and never where it would endanger the tenant's health or safety (C.R.S. 38-12-506). A clause in the lease isn't enough. State habitability law leaves out a few arrangements, unless they were set up to avoid it, such as a cabin in an unincorporated area rented for recreation without public water, heat and sewer service, and premises the occupant uses mainly for agriculture (C.R.S. 38-12-511). Mobile home park spaces are left out too, but park law has its own sewer duties for the landlord (C.R.S. 38-12-212.3).

Cleaning the septic system must be done by a county-licensed systems cleaner (section 30-4-120), and repairs need a county permit (section 30-4-30), whoever is assigned the work.
